newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil coffee exporter groups discuss unification.
newsitem.headline: Brazil coffee exporter groups discuss unification.

text.p: The first set of talks yesterday on whether and how to unite Brazil's two exporter groups at least made clear the two associations want unification but negotiations may take some time, exporter officials said.
"What we want and they want is to unite. That part is clear," Oswaldo Aranha, president of the Brazilian Coffee Exporters' Federation (Febec), said.
"The will exits on both sides to form one group but it is difficult," said Jorge Esteve, president of the Brazilian Coffee Exporters Association (Abecafe).
Febec is Brazil's traditional exporters' group but in November 1995 a group of exporters formed Abecafe, principally because they opposed a plan dividing out exports internally.
The association has grown in size and now has 45 members, accounting for around 47 percent of Brazilian coffee exports in 1996, according to Abecafe statistics.
One of the main points of division last year was the creation of Brazil's new coffee council, called the CDPC, which united the private coffee sector and government officials.
However only one place was alloted to the exporting sector, with Febec officially chosen as the representative exporters' body which resulted in a wave of protests from Abecafe.
Last month Febec officials agreed to begin talks to see if there was a way of uniting the two groups and a six-member commission was formed to discuss the issue.
Elections of Febec officers, due to have been held at the end of last month, have been delayed until end-May in anticipation of the creation of a new body.
But given the commission will only now again meet at the end May, elections may need to be delayed further, Aranha said.

Points of divergence between the two groups are where any new entity would be based and whether it should be a federation of the existing coffee associations or a separate body which individual export companies would join.

Otherwise this week the main talking point in the market was the continuing widening of differentials as the internal market's slower rise allowed exporters to offer Brazils at bargain prices in comparison to Central Americans.

Swedish qualities which last week were quoted at 15 under for May/June shipment are now been quoted at a 28 point differential while full description 17/18s are currently offered at around 15 under against last week's 8 point discount.
"The problem is roasters calculate that taking 50 percent Centrals and 50 percent robustas, it is still cheaper than 100 percent Brazilians," one trader said.
However demand could soon start picking up again as supplies from Colombia and Central America trickle out, said Santos export firm Icatu/Sumatra.

"The feeling we have...is that the demand is and will be picking up considerably again since Brazils, from being a "filler" for most blends, will be a "super elastic bonder" for whatever is left of Centrals," Icatu/Sumatra said in a report.

In some ways the Brazilian government must be hoping this demand does not come earlier than expected and boost May/June exports given traders' increasing belief Brazil will exceed its limit set by the Association of Coffee Producing Countries.
The May 9 Rio de Janeiro Coffee Center Bulletin put April to June export registrations at 3.39 million bags as of May 2.

This would give a total of up to 7.28 million bags given January-March exports of 3.89 million bags and while traders warn registrations are not necessarily a definite indication of shipments, estimates range between 6.5 million and 7.5 million.

With an upcoming council session of the producer association on May 21, dealers anticipate goverment officials may try and either anticipate any 1997/98 quotas or simply ask Brazil's 1996/97 six million bag export quota be increased.
((-Rio de Janeiro newsroom, 5521 5074151))
